Iran Claims Two More Oil Tankers Hit Mines in Strait of Hormuz
Two oil tankers exploded and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after hitting naval mines while attempting to transit the chokepoint via a southern route not authorized by Iran, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Monday, as Iranian reports of such incidents have intensified in recent days.
The two tankers had attempted to pass through the route under the direct guidance of U.S. officers and with the support of U.S. military fighter jets, the IRGC Navy said in a statement carried by Iranian Mehr news agency.
On Sunday and Monday alone, a total of six oil tankers caught fire and sank in the Strait of Hormuz, according to the IRGC Navy, which added that pollution caused by the explosions had spread across the coastal areas and waters of the Strait.
"The IRGC Navy described the actions as punitive measures in response to the U.S. military's illegal blockade and violations of Iran's regulations governing the Strait of Hormuz," the Mehr news agency reported.
Moreover, the IRGC Navy warned oil tanker and oil firm owners that "the U.S.-backed southern passage through the strait had been mined, cautioning that trusting U.S. military officials and cooperating with them would put their vessels at risk."
For days, Iran has been reporting nearly daily incidents with tankers hitting naval mines in corridors that Iran has designated as "unauthorized" in the Strait of Hormuz.
Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran's top negotiator and Parliament Speaker, told Al Jazeera in an exclusive interview last week that the Strait of Hormuz navigation would not return to pre-war conditions, ever.
"There are no 'free waters' [international waters] there, and the 1982 [UN Convention on the Law of the Sea] does not apply to the strait … The regulations within the Strait of Hormuz are governed by the laws of the two littoral states that border it," the official told Al Jazeera.

items.title: China confirms Xi-Trump-Putin historic summit. What will be on the agenda?
items.summary: The talks are expected to focus on issues including nuclear non-proliferation, the Middle East war, trade policies and, possibly, the Ukraine war.
items.content:
China confirms Xi-Trump-Putin meeting in first three-way summit
The talks are expected to focus on issues including nuclear non-proliferation, the Middle East war, trade policies and, possibly, the Ukraine war.
The three-way summit among the three nations is unprecedented.
"The ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table, a first-among-equals scenario, will deliver much of the political benefit" for Beijing: analyst.
Russian artist Alexey Sergienko unveils his new pop art painting dubbed "Shenzhen, 26" in Saint Petersburg on November 12, 2026.
China confirmed Monday that President Xi Jinping will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump in Shenzhen on Thursday, setting up the first-ever gathering of the three leaders.
That confirmation from a spokesperson at China's Foreign Ministry follows announcements from Moscow and the White House. The Wall Street Journal had reported last month that Putin had proposed a three-way sit-down in an attempt to negotiate an end to the four-year war in Ukraine.
While the summit among the three nations, on the sidelines of the APEC meeting in Shenzhen, is unprecedented, the leaders have held bilateral meetings over the years. Xi has met with Trump three times since October last year and more than 40 times with Putin since becoming president in 2013. Trump and Putin have met in person on several occasions, including a visit to Alaska by the Russian leader in August 2025.
"For Xi, just the ability to bring Putin and Trump to the table, a first among equals scenario, will deliver much of the political benefit even before the discussions begin," said Peter Alexander, Shanghai-based managing director at Z-Ben Advisors.
Trump has departed Washington, D.C. for a four-day trip to Asia that also includes a stop in the Philippines.
The main hurdle to the first-of-its-kind summit now appears to be "a disagreement over the agenda," said Neo Wang, chief China strategist at Evercore ISI.
The White House signaled the U.S. intention to prioritize talks over nuclear non-proliferation and the Middle East war, while downplaying the prospects of engaging in talks over Ukraine — a topic high on Moscow's agenda.
"He [Trump] will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world , whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman, told reporters on a briefing call . The president will raise the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran in the meeting but is not expected to bring up Russia's war in Ukraine, the official said.
China has no interest in engaging in nuclear disarmament talks until it achieves parity with the U.S. in about 10 years, said David Roche, strategist at Quantum Strategy.
Chances of Jensen Huang returning to Nvidia 'very slim': David Roche
Putin's position on the war appears unwavering, with the Russian president telling U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff in a meeting in Moscow last week that Europe should "figure out" whether "they want peace or war." The meeting came a day after an earlier round of talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine wrapped up in Abu Dhabi.
Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov said last week the talks in Shenzhen would continue the diplomatic efforts aimed at reaching a negotiated settlement to the Ukraine war, according to state-controlled local media Russia Today.
The summit will likely yield little concrete result, but presents an "almost 100% photo op" that lifts China's status and power at the top table, said Roche, while Trump's political standing slides. Nvidia and the chip-smuggling issues involving a suspected Chinese spy will stay off the agenda, as Trump steers clear of thorny issues where he is unlikely to claim success.
China and Russia could turn more aggressive with their military ambitions over the next two years if they perceive Trump as politically weakened, Brookings Institution senior fellow Robert Kagan told CNBC earlier this month, following the dramatic defeat of Trump's Republican Party in the midterm election.
China did not specify what will be discussed at the three leaders' meeting in Monday's statement.
"Xi may be inclined to do Putin a favor by showing up, given close strategic ties," said Wang. But a joint statement on Ukraine territory, security arrangements or sanctions against Russia appears unlikely, he said, as it would leave Beijing "more exposed to political scrutiny and accountability."
A U.S.-China trade truce set to expire in January is likely to be on the table, with analysts largely expecting an extension despite signs of growing friction in the bilateral relationship.
Aside from an immediate extension, leaders may also look to assess "whether a more durable framework for a rebalancing of U.S.–China trade relations can be established," said Carlos Casanova, senior economist for Asia at UBP.
U.S. trade deficit with China remains substantial, with Beijing's exports to Washington recording double-digit growth for most of this year, from last year's low base. Narrowing that deficit will be central to Washington's call for a more balanced trade, Casanova said.

What the F Fund? Bond losses, rate hikes and the G Fund temptation
This episode of Fed Thread puts into plain-speak what’s happening with bonds, interest rates and the TSP’s G and F funds.
The G Fund has one very appealing quality right now in that it doesn’t lose principal. Meanwhile, the F Fund has been taking a beating, and anyone watching their TSP balance shrink might be wondering why they’re still holding it.
It’s an understandable temptation. But what if moving to the safer-looking option means giving up an opportunity that could be just around the corner?
That’s the dilemma at the center of this episode of Fed Thread , where certified financial planners Evan Radin and Neil Cain of Capital Financial Planners put into plain-speak what’s happening with bonds, interest rates and the TSP’s G and F funds.
Before you make the G Fund leap, they suggest there’s more to consider than which fund has performed better lately. Here are three questions worth asking yourself before doing anything:
The G and F Funds may both fall into the conservative investment category, but they work very differently.
The G Fund protects your principal and pays interest that resets monthly. The F Fund, on the other hand, tracks the broader U.S. investment-grade bond market, which means its value can fluctuate as interest rates change.
The catch is that when interest rates rise, existing bond prices generally fall. Then when rates move in the opposite direction, those same bonds can become more valuable.
That’s why Radin and Cain caution against judging the F Fund solely by its recent performance. If interest rates begin to decline, investors who abandoned bonds after a period of losses could miss some of the recovery.
Essentially, the G Fund’s stability is appealing, but that doesn’t automatically make it the better long-term choice.
This may be the most practical question of the three. Rather than trying to predict what the market or Federal Reserve will do next, Cain suggests looking at when you’ll need to withdraw your money.
If you’re expecting to draw from your TSP over the next one to three years, he says that money may belong in the G Fund, where principal won’t fluctuate with interest rates. Money you don’t anticipate needing for several years may have a different role in your portfolio.
That also matters for retirees considering the L Income Fund. Its conservative allocation may make sense for someone who needs regular withdrawals or simply can’t tolerate much market fluctuation, but it may be more conservative than necessary for others.
In essence, Radin and Cain recommend that your investment choices reflect your spending needs, not just your comfort level with today’s headlines.
Am I being too conservative, or not conservative enough?
It’s easy to focus on the risk of losing money, but the other risk that can sneak up on investors is being so conservative that their savings don’t keep pace with inflation.
Radin says he’s seeing clients on both ends of the spectrum. Some became overly conservative after getting spooked by market volatility, while others are taking on more risk chasing recent returns.
Neither reaction necessarily makes for a sound retirement strategy, and bonds aren’t a guaranteed hedge, either. Cain points to 2022, when inflation drove both stocks and bonds lower, showing that the economic conditions behind a market downturn matter just as much as the downturn itself.
The key lesson is to not let a bad stretch in the F Fund, a tempting G Fund rate or an unsettling market headline make the decision for you. Understand what each investment is designed to do, consider when you’ll need your money and make sure your overall allocation supports the retirement you’re planning for.
Sometimes the biggest investment mistake isn’t choosing the wrong fund, it’s making the right move at the wrong time.

If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming in 2027, Warren Buffett’s Advice Makes My Next Move Clear
Volatility has returned to the stock market. Since hitting a record high on Oct. 6, 2026, the Nasdaq Composite has dropped more than 10%. That leaves many investors asking a rational, if concerning, question: Is a stock market crash on the horizon?
This anxiety leads many investors to pull up stakes and retreat from the market altogether. That strategy creates a new problem: when to get back into the market.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
Therefore, I would suggest that during volatile periods – like right now – investors should take a page from Warren Buffett's playbook. Namely, build an investing strategy and schedule that can withstand volatility. Here's how to do it.
First things first, investors don't need to be fortune tellers. Indeed, even if someone could accurately predict market crashes , they would still need to accurately predict market bottoms – something that is just as unlikely as predicting tops.
A better strategy accepts that negative outcomes are inevitable, but rare, and can be mitigated with some planning.
To illustrate, think of someone who enjoys spending time outdoors but wants to avoid getting soaked by the rain. They could be 100% sure to avoid the rain by canceling every outdoor activity for the next year, but that would be a massive hassle. Conversely, they could simply check the weather forecast each morning and carry an umbrella on days when the chance of rain is high.
Once investors have planned for downturns, they can focus on which investments best carry them safely through volatile periods. Here, it's best to turn directly to the Oracle of Omaha for advice.
Rather than chasing short-term market fads, Buffett has advised investors to take long-term positions in real businesses they can easily understand. That's why Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE:BRKB) (NYSE:BRKA) has owned large stakes in companies like Coca-Cola (NYSE:KO), American Express (NYSE:AXP), and Moody's (NYSE:MCO) for decades.
By stretching the time horizon out to 10, 20, 30 years or more, recent interest rate movements, unemployment reports, and GDP forecasts all fade in importance. Over long periods, what matters most is whether a company's business model is resilient and whether its management team is guiding it properly.
To borrow a line from Buffett himself, he quipped that he looks for companies so wonderful that "an idiot can run them, because sooner or later, one will."
Once you have the right mindset and the right stocks on your watch list, it's time to talk execution. A great strategy will still fail if it's not executed properly. Therefore, it's best to write rules that can be followed – even on a bad day.
Start small. If a person can only put $10 in the market each month, it's better than nothing. Raise the contribution amount when possible. Ensure there's an emergency reserve, separate from investment funds, for unexpected bills, large purchases, and similar expenses.
Finally, remember that investing during volatile periods can be emotionally taxing. Find ways to see the bright side when the market is moving lower. If a normal monthly contribution of $100 normally buys 1 share of stock, remind yourself that during volatile periods, $100 might buy 1.5 shares. Over time, those additional shares will add up.
No one knows what 2027 holds. A stock market crash could be on the way, but that won't keep anyone from investing. Instead, stick to the investing strategy and rules laid out by one of the best to ever do it: Contribute regularly, invest in great companies, and play the long game.
Over time, that strategy made Warren Buffett one of the wealthiest people on the planet, and it can no doubt help many others achieve their financial goals – regardless of whether a stock market crash is on the horizon.

If the Stock Market Crashes, Warren Buffett Says This is the Best Move Investors Can Make
The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) has advanced 10% year to date amid remarkably strong earnings growth driven by the artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out. Yet, investors have become increasingly pessimistic throughout the year, raising a familiar question: What should you do if the market takes a turn for the worse?
Warren Buffett has addressed this question repeatedly. His advice starts with accepting that steep declines are part of stock ownership. No one can reliably predict when the next crash will happen, but investors can decide in advance how they will respond.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
Bearish sentiment has increased sharply throughout the year
Weekly surveys conducted by the American Association of Individual Investors (AAII) show that bearish sentiment -- the percentage of investors who expect the stock market to decline over the next six months -- increased from 27% in January to 51% in November.
Possible explanations include doubts about the durability of the artificial intelligence boom and whether the profits it generates will justify massive infrastructure spending. Midterms may have added to those concerns, as several incoming governors and members of Congress support data center restrictions, including moratoriums on construction projects.
Meanwhile, high energy prices tied to the Iran conflict and tariffs imposed by President Trump have contributed to inflation. The Federal Reserve raised interest rates in September, and the market expects another hike in December, according to CME Group 's FedWatch tool. Higher rates make bonds more attractive, which can pull money away from stocks.
Any of those pressures could deepen the recent sell-off. But even if the stock market recovers in the near term, the next severe downturn is inevitable. So, it makes sense to have a plan in place before it arrives.
Warren Buffett's advice is to buy good businesses when pessimism creates bargains
Stock market downturns can make selling seem like the safest move. But Warren Buffett has repeatedly explained that falling prices are actually an opportunity for patient investors to purchase stock in their favorite companies at a discount.
"Widespread fear is your friend as an investor, because it serves up bargain purchases," he wrote in his 2016 shareholder letter. That sentiment is particularly relevant today given that investors have become increasingly bearish throughout the year. That hard part is deciding where to invest your money.
Buffett answered that question in his 1996 letter. "Your goal as an investor should simply be to purchase, at a rational price, a part interest in an easily-understandable business whose earnings are virtually certain to be materially higher five, ten, and twenty years from now."
That quote is jam-packed with good advice. First, Buffett makes it clear that price matters. Second, investors must understand a company before buying shares. Third, investors should only consider stocks whose earnings are likely to be much higher in the future.
Drawdowns have historically been an excellent opportunity to buy stocks
The Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) recently entered correction territory , and similar downturns in the past reveal an encouraging pattern. During the last decade, the Nasdaq returned an average of 21% over the 12-month period following its first close in correction territory.
The S&P 500 is not currently in correction territory, but it has displayed a similar resilience during past downturns. Specifically, during the last decade, the S&P 500 has returned an average of 18% over the 12-month period following its first close in correction territory.
Here's the bottom line: Market downturns are part of the investing experience. But history says stocks will eventually recover and Buffett's advice provides a clear plan: Focus on understandable businesses with strong long-term growth prospects, and buy when shares trade at sensible prices.
If the stock market crashes tomorrow, investors should put that advice into action. And they should plan to hold any stocks they buy for at least five years. Buffett once said, "All there is to investing is picking good stocks at good times and staying with them as long as they remain good companies.

Europe Has Already Drained 10% of Its Summer Gas Injections
Europe has not only entered the heating season with the lowest gas levels in storage sites in decades, but it has also withdrawn in recent weeks 10% of the natural gas injected during the summer filling season, leaving supply vulnerable to potentially extreme cold winter weather.
So far into the heating season, which has just started, the net withdrawals of European countries have reached about 10% of the 51.2 billion cubic meters of gas they had injected into storage sites this summer, Azeri outlet APA-Economics reports , quoting data from Gas Infrastructure Europe.
The EU has an eased target to fill storage facilities to 90% at some point between October 1 and December 1, with a possible 10 percentage-point deviation from the target in case of difficulties in filling capacity.
This summer has been one of these difficult periods for gas injections as European operators had to pay hefty sums for LNG supply and compete with Asia for spot cargoes after the Iran war halted nearly all shipments from Qatar.
Before the heating season began, the most Europe managed was to have gas storage sites only about 76% full, considerably lower compared to about 90% in previous years.
Net withdrawals started in the middle of October and accelerated toward early November, before easing in the past week, data from Gas Infrastructure Europe showed .
A separate dataset by GIE showed that the EU's gas storage sites were only 70.5% full as of November 15, compared to a five-year average of 89% and about 82% at this time last year.
At the end of October, Europe's benchmark natural gas price hit a four-year high as temperatures began to drop and net withdrawals accelerated, while much of Qatar's LNG is still trapped at the Strait of Hormuz.
INES, the association of gas storage system operators in Europe's biggest economy, Germany, last week warned that "gas supply in Germany may not be fully secured during the coming winter in the event of extremely cold temperatures. INES sees an urgent need to strengthen the strategic framework for winter preparedness."

Nasdaq Stock Market Correction: These 6 Words From Warren Buffett Are More Relevant Than Ever
After years of unusually high gains fueled by artificial intelligence (AI) stocks, the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) recently entered correction territory as investors reassess the outlook for the AI industry.
On Oct. 6, the Nasdaq reached a record closing high of 27,599. By Nov. 5, the index had fallen to 24,315, representing a 12% decline. Although the Nasdaq has recovered a bit, the tech-heavy index still sits roughly 8% below its record.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
This turbulence has created an interesting dilemma for investors. Should you sell your stocks before another potential drawdown, or take advantage of falling share prices?
Luckily, Warren Buffett offered an answer decades ago. One of his most famous investing principles is particularly relevant today.
The technology sector is facing several overlapping challenges. First, November's midterm elections resulted in Democrats winning control of both chambers of Congress. Throughout the campaign, electricity affordability, data center construction, and the environmental impact of AI infrastructure became a prominent political issue.
With Democrats assuming congressional control in January, investors are evaluating the possibility of increased regulatory scrutiny and changes to infrastructure permitting. This matters for hyperscalers like Microsoft , Amazon , Alphabet , and Meta Platforms , which have collectively committed hundreds of billions of dollars of capital to build data centers.
If new regulations lead to rising costs or project delays, big tech may choose to slow down their infrastructure spending. In turn, this could flow downstream and affect semiconductor manufacturers and other businesses supporting the AI ecosystem. Of course, potential policy changes have not yet materialized. Moreover, congressional control does not automatically translate into restrictions on data center development.
Another concern weighing on the Nasdaq involves Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA). On Nov. 12, the company's founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned following reports concerning his personal relationships and questions surrounding potential foreign-intelligence compromises.
Nvidia's board of directors appointed CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement. The leadership transition introduces uncertainty for perhaps the most influential company in the AI industry.
Nvidia's scandals have also fueled scrutiny around other semiconductor companies and the broader AI landscape.
Throughout his career, Buffett consistently emphasized the importance of separating a company's underlying value from short-term fluctuations in its stock price. In Berkshire Hathaway 's 1986 shareholder letter, he explained his approach with six simple words: "Be greedy when others are fearful."
This philosophy has become a cornerstone of value investing. Buffett doesn't view falling stock prices as an automatic reason to sell. Rather, the "Oracle of Omaha" evaluates whether a company's competitive advantages, earnings potential, and long-term intrinsic value remain intact.
If a financially strong business suddenly begins trading at a discount to its intrinsic value, market volatility can actually create an attractive opportunity to buy the dip.
Here's what investors should do during the Nasdaq correction
The goal is to identify businesses with durable economic moats, strong balance sheets, dependable cash flow, and attractive long-term growth prospects. Consider companies such as Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, and Nvidia.
These businesses all have competitive advantages, including strong customer relationships, proprietary technologies, established ecosystems, and significant financial flexibility. Although their stock prices may fluctuate with changing expectations about the pace of AI spending, their underlying businesses are not necessarily deteriorating at the same pace.
This creates an arbitrage opportunity to purchase high-quality businesses at more reasonable valuations. By gradually building positions through dollar-cost averaging, investors can reduce the risks associated with investing a large sum immediately before another sell-off.
Most importantly, investors should maintain a long-term perspective. As the chart below illustrates, the stock market has endured its share of setbacks. The grey columns represent recessions, including those witnessed during the aftermath of the dot-com bubble, the Great Recession, and the COVID-19 pandemic.
The theme here is that the Nasdaq eventually recovered and established new record highs. These trends underscore the importance of remaining invested through volatility. In the long run, history suggests the Nasdaq's correction will look like another temporary setback in the stock market's long-term upward trajectory.

Oil falls below $94 as supply surplus outweighs renewed risks in Hormuz
Brent crude fell about 2% on Monday, hovering slightly above a two-month low reached last week.
Oil tanker and tugboats are visible alongside the Donges industrial terminal on the Loire estuary in Donges in Loire Atlantique in Pays de la Loire, in France, on Sept. 25 2026. — Andre Bourriquen / Hans Lucas / AFP via Getty Images
Oil prices fell Monday as a rebound in global supply overshadowed fresh Iranian threats and signs of a renewed US military buildup in the Gulf.
What happened: Brent crude was trading at $93.53 per barrel on Monday as of 11:13 am EST, down about 2% on the day and hovering slightly above a two-month low reached last week.
Prices remain well below levels from late October, when barrels of Brent nearly reached $120 just ahead of US elections on Nov. 3 amid fears that the conflict would escalate in coming weeks. Yet benchmark prices quickly sank below $100 after the vote, with sweeping Democratic gains raising expectations that President Donald Trump would face pressure to wind down the war.
Even as prices fell Monday, a tanker was struck in the Strait of Hormuz. The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported that the vessel was heading out of the strait when an unknown projectile hit it, causing an engine room fire. No casualties were reported.

OPEC+ capacity review could reshape global oil production limits
capacity review , global oil production , Middle East , OPEC
(Oil & Gas 360) – Officials from the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) met virtually Monday to discuss a review of members' maximum sustainable oil production capacity, an assessment expected to influence production quotas for 2027. The discussions come as recovering Middle Eastern crude supplies and expectations of a global oil surplus complicate efforts to balance output among the world's major petroleum exporters.
OPEC confirmed the meeting through its official social media account but did not disclose specific decisions or conclusions. The review covers members of OPEC and the broader OPEC+ alliance, which includes Russia and other producers cooperating on oil supply management.
Maximum sustainable production capacity measures how much crude a country can maintain over an extended period under normal operating conditions. The assessment differs from actual production, which may be constrained by voluntary cuts, infrastructure disruptions, sanctions or geopolitical developments.
The review is particularly important because OPEC+ intends to use updated capacity estimates as a reference for establishing 2027 production baselines. Those baselines help determine individual output allocations and could influence future adjustments to collective production targets.
Originally scheduled for completion by September, the assessment was delayed after the conflict involving Iran disrupted oil infrastructure and capacity expansion projects across the Middle East. U.S. petroleum consultancy DeGolyer and MacNaughton has been conducting independent evaluations for participating producers, excluding Russia, Iran and Venezuela because of U.S. sanctions.
The process has exposed differences among producers seeking to protect or increase their production allocations. Iraq has pursued higher output limits, while countries with substantial capacity investments have sought recognition for their ability to produce additional barrels. The United Arab Emirates, which previously advocated higher quotas, withdrew from OPEC in May.
The negotiations are taking place against a changing global supply outlook. The International Energy Agency expects petroleum supply to exceed demand during the fourth quarter as Middle Eastern exports recover from earlier disruptions. Additional production could intensify downward pressure on crude prices if demand growth remains insufficient to absorb returning barrels.
OPEC+ maintained its December production targets at a November 1 meeting, postponing broader decisions until its scheduled November 29 ministerial gathering. The group must also consider the future of approximately 2 million barrels per day in existing production restrictions extending through the end of 2026.
For oil producers outside OPEC+, including U.S. shale operators and Canadian exploration and production companies, the outcome could influence crude price expectations, drilling activity and capital allocation. Higher collective production targets could increase competition for market share, while more restrictive quotas might provide additional price support.
For institutional investors and family offices, the capacity review offers insight into the potential direction of global oil supply management. Differences between assessed capacity, actual production and available export infrastructure will be important when evaluating whether announced quotas can translate into physical barrels.
The November 29 meeting will provide a clearer indication of how OPEC+ intends to balance competing production interests against the possibility of excess global supply in 2027. The resulting framework could shape crude price expectations and upstream investment decisions well beyond the coming year.

Oil tanker rates tumble as Gulf crude shipments rebound
geopolitical risk premiums , Gulf crude shipments , oil tanker rates , rebound
(Oil & Gas 360) – Global supertanker freight rates have fallen more than 60% from October's record highs as recovering Middle Eastern crude exports reduce demand for longer-distance oil shipments and ease some of the geopolitical risk premiums that drove transportation costs sharply higher.
The decline reflects a changing global petroleum trade environment as exporters restore supply flows despite continuing security threats around the Strait of Hormuz.
According to Baltic Exchange data, freight rates for very large crude carriers (VLCCs) transporting oil from the Gulf of Oman to China declined to approximately 308 Worldscale points on November 13, down 64% from a record 841 points on October 8. Worldscale is an industry freight-rate benchmark rather than a direct measure of daily vessel earnings.
The sharp correction follows several months of elevated transportation costs associated with the conflict involving the United States, Israel and Iran. Attacks on commercial vessels and disruptions to traditional shipping routes forced petroleum traders to reorganize cargo movements, increasing demand for tanker capacity and pushing freight rates to extraordinary levels.
Middle Eastern exporters have since restored crude shipments to levels approaching those recorded before the conflict. Alternative transportation arrangements, including ship-to-ship transfers and voyages with vessel tracking systems disabled, have supported the recovery, even as security threats persist.
As more Gulf crude becomes available to Asian refiners, demand for oil transported over longer distances from the United States, West Africa and the North Sea has weakened. Those changes reduce the number of vessel-days required to move equivalent crude volumes, freeing up tanker capacity and placing downward pressure on charter rates.
The effect has extended beyond Middle Eastern shipping routes. Freight rates for tankers carrying West African crude to Asia have also declined sharply, reflecting reduced demand for long-haul voyages and increased vessel availability as ships complete deliveries in Asian markets.
The decline is not solely attributable to improving physical supply conditions. Analysts at Arrow Shipbroking have indicated that the speed of the correction also reflects an unwinding of the geopolitical risk premium that developed when vessel attacks and uncertainty surrounding the Strait of Hormuz intensified.
For tanker owners and shipping investors, lower spot freight rates could reduce earnings expectations following an exceptionally profitable period. Companies with substantial exposure to spot charter markets may experience greater volatility than operators with vessels committed under longer-term contracts.
For oil producers and refiners, declining transportation costs could improve the economics of international crude movements, although the benefits will vary by location, contract structure and prevailing commodity prices. Lower freight expenses may also narrow regional crude price differentials and influence purchasing decisions among Asian refiners.
The broader oil market is experiencing similar adjustments. Crude prices have declined as Middle Eastern exports recover, while the International Energy Agency expects global petroleum supply to exceed demand during the fourth quarter.
For energy investors, the rapid reversal in tanker rates illustrates how changes in shipping patterns can amplify movements in petroleum markets. A sustained reduction in freight costs could benefit crude buyers while pressuring tanker operator profitability, but renewed attacks or transportation disruptions could quickly reverse the trend.
The outlook will depend on the durability of Middle Eastern export recovery, vessel availability, Asian crude purchasing patterns and the security of shipping routes through the Persian Gulf.

Gold Falls Below $3,900 as Stronger Dollar and Fed Rate Expectations Pressure Precious Metals
Fine gold ©Hamiltonleen Gold prices extended their decline on Monday, remaining below $3,900 per ounce as a firmer US dollar and expectations of further interest rate increases by the Federal Reserve weighed on precious metals.
At 00:10 ET (05:10 GMT), spot gold (XAU/USD) fell 0.4% to $3,868.88 per ounce, while gold futures declined 0.3% to $3,871.92.
Other precious metals also recorded losses. Spot silver (XAG/USD) dropped 2.1% to $47.7430 per ounce, while platinum (XPT/USD) declined 1.3% to $1,473.49.
Spot palladium (XPD/USD) fell 1.4% to $985.81, while palladium futures decreased 1.6% to $984.25.
Meanwhile, the US Dollar Index advanced 0.03% to 103.44, adding pressure to dollar-denominated commodities.
Gold had already fallen 4.5% during the previous week, reaching its lowest level in more than a year as higher oil prices contributed to inflation concerns and expectations that US borrowing costs would remain elevated.
US Inflation Data Reinforces Expectations of Further Rate Increases
Recent US economic data has strengthened expectations that the Federal Reserve will continue tightening monetary policy.
Producer prices accelerated in October, recording their largest annual increase in four years. The figures added to concerns about persistent inflation and supported expectations of another interest rate increase at the Federal Reserve's December meeting.
Several central bank officials have also indicated that further action may be necessary to bring inflation under control.
Kansas City Federal Reserve President Jeff Schmid said on Sunday that inflation was still "running too hot" and that policymakers had "some work to do" to address continuing price pressures.
Federal Reserve Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said on Friday that inflation had become the main consideration in his monetary policy assessment, with economic growth continuing and labour market conditions showing signs of stabilisation.
His comments suggested support for additional interest rate increases.
Boston Federal Reserve President Susan Collins also indicated that tighter monetary policy could be required, suggesting that borrowing costs might need to rise further than she had previously expected.
Higher interest rates generally increase the opportunity cost of holding gold, which does not provide interest income, while a stronger dollar can make the metal more expensive for buyers using other currencies.
Markets Price in December Federal Reserve Rate Increase
Financial markets are assigning a high probability to another US interest rate increase in December.
According to CME Group's FedWatch tool, traders are pricing in a 94% probability of a 25-basis-point increase at the Federal Reserve's next policy meeting.
The remaining 6% probability is assigned to a larger increase of 50 basis points.
Some investors also anticipate that the central bank could continue raising borrowing costs beyond December if inflation remains elevated.
Attention will now turn to Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, who is scheduled to speak later on Monday.
Investors will also examine the minutes from the Federal Open Market Committee's October meeting, due for publication on Wednesday, for further indications about the direction of monetary policy.
Geopolitical developments in the Middle East also remained under scrutiny following reports of further military activity involving Iran and regional forces.
On Sunday, Saudi-backed forces reportedly retreated during fighting against Iran-aligned Houthi rebels in Yemen.
Separately, Iran was reported to have launched drone attacks against US military bases in Bahrain.
The developments added to uncertainty surrounding regional security and energy markets, although expectations of higher US interest rates and dollar strength remained the principal factors affecting gold prices during Monday's trading.

items.title: Aschenbrenner’s Situational Awareness made AI bets again before October rout
items.summary: Leopold Aschenbrenner's hedge fund, which almost collapsed over the summer, bought AI stocks before shares began tumbling.
items.content:
Situational Awareness' latest 13F filing shows a renewed public-markets book concentrated in AI-linked stocks and options even after the fund’s near collapse in July.
The filing does not show whether the fund kept or sold those positions during the October sell-off.
AI stocks have suffered in recent weeks amid worries about financing for the buildout as well as a potential slowdown in its development following the midterm election results.
Leopold Aschenbrenner's artificial intelligence-themed hedge fund Situational Awareness, which nearly collapsed in July, loaded back up on AI stocks as it returned to the financial markets at the end of the third quarter. But all of its holdings are down big the last month and a half.
According to a new regulatory filing, as the fund got back on its feet Aschenbrenner took an equity position in Australian neocloud company SharonAI valued at more than $440 million, along with equity stakes in AI-centric plays Cleanspark , IREN , Bitdeer Technologies and Fermi . The Cleanspark stake is worth almost $39 million, while Iren and Bitdeer stakes are more than $21 million and more than $20 million, respectively. Fermi, meanwhile, has a value of more than $11 million.
The fund also owned call options at the end of September in neocloud Nebius , memory chip name Sandisk , the Roundhill Memory ETF (DRAM) and data center power play Bloom Energy . Sandisk and Nebius were key holdings that almost took out his fund over the summer.
All of these Situational Awareness holdings have been routed since Sept. 30. SharonAI is at the top of that list, seeing a 58% loss in October. It's also fallen 11% so far this month. IREN was down 41% in October, while Nebius declined 35%. Last week, Nebius plummeted more than 16% in a single day after the company issued a weak full-year forecast .
It's not known whether the hedge fund manager got out of those positions during the October AI selloff. The 13F filing is just a snapshot of what the hedge fund held at the end of the quarter.
Aschenbrenner — who launched the fund in 2024 after rising to fame that same year with his AI manifesto also entitled Situational Awareness — re-entered financial markets a bit in September, sources told CNBC at the time.
The Monday filing shows he picked up right where he left off.
The near-collapse of his hedge fund over the summer forced him to sell all of its public equity positions to Ken Griffin's Citadel. The fund had $45 billion in assets at its peak, but that tumbled to around $10 billion , consisting mostly of private stakes.
Stocked tethered to the AI trade took a hit in the most recent quarter as investors grew concerned about a slowdown in development of the technology . Those fears were spurred by comments from industry leaders such as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman back in September, with the latter saying that the company going public this year would be "ill-advised."
Since then, pressure on the trade has only continued.
In recent weeks, investors have worried about how Democratic wins in the midterm elections could hinder data center development , whether some technology companies are using too much debt to finance the AI buildout and what role Nvidia will play in that financing with Jensen Huang now out as CEO at the company .
Losses in Nvidia as well as other AI-related stocks dragged down the three leading U.S. indexes during Monday's session as investors continued to assess the fallout of Huang's departure.

Cantwell calls on Lutnick to stop AI chip sales to China
Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., the ranking member on the Senate commerce panel, is urging Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to use his authority to stop the flow of advanced AI chips to companies with ties to China.
Lutnick has drawn scrutiny since news broke about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and reports that the commerce secretary slow-walked attempts to crack down on the sale of restricted chips to China.
Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., who chairs the Senate banking committee, has called Lutnick to testify before Congress in December.
Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) speaks during a press conference following the weekly policy luncheon, on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., June 3, 2025.
Sen. Maria Cantwell , the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, alleged in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday that the department under his leadership failed to prevent China from accessing the U.S.'s most advanced artificial intelligence chips.
In the letter, Cantwell prodded Lutnick to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving the technology. She sent the missive ahead of a planned meeting this week between U.S. officials and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, in China.
Her urging comes as Washington reels from revelations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading U.S. company designing advanced AI chips.

Alice Huang was an executive at Singaporean technology company Megaspeed that allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China.
Lutnick, meanwhile, has come under fire for stalling efforts to crack down on chip sales to China and for his close personal relationship with Jensen Huang, who was a vocal opponent of export controls.
"The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology," Cantwell wrote to Lutnick. "These failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI."
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.
Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority to enforce a 2018 law, known as the Export Control Reform Act , which gives the Commerce Department broad latitude to enforce export controls and protect sensitive American technology.
She also cites potential financial conflicts involving Lutnick's sons , who control Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination. And she notes the Trump administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, which she said could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology."
"America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," Cantwell wrote.
Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress have ramped up pressure on Lutnick and other Commerce Department officials after a Nov. 9 New York Times report alleging the department may have slow-walked an investigation into Megaspeed.
On Thursday, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December.
Lutnick has agreed to appear before the panel, Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement last week.
And Democrats, who will take control of both the House and Senate in January, have signaled they will investigate Jensen Huang and Commerce officials.
On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the top Democrat on the Senate banking panel, and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
The letter gives all three officials until Nov. 17 to confirm that preservation directives have been issued.

Stock Market Midday, Nov. 16: Nasdaq Tumbles as Wall Street Braces for Nvidia Earnings and Bitcoin Slides
Wall Street extended its recent losses on Monday, November 16, as mounting selling pressure across technology and cryptocurrency markets weighed on investor sentiment ahead of Nvidia's highly anticipated earnings report. As of 11:31 a.m. ET, the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) led major indexes lower, falling 1.34% to 24,799, while the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) declined 0.99% to 7,487. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI) slipped 0.60% to 52,032.
Selling pressure extended beyond equities, with gold declining 0.61% to $3,862.60 and Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) falling to its lowest level since July. Meanwhile, the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield climbed to 5.15%, placing additional pressure on equity valuations. Sector performance remained mixed, with real estate leading gains and communication services suffering the steepest losses.
Tyson Foods (NYSE:TSN) bucked the broader market sell-off, jumping 7.01% after the meat producer's encouraging fiscal 2027 guidance overshadowed a fourth-quarter earnings miss.
Meanwhile, Strategy (NASDAQ:MSTR), formerly MicroStrategy, plunged 6.78% as Bitcoin extended its recent losses. Investors are also weighing the potential selling pressure associated with the company's removal from MSCI's equity indexes, which could reduce passive investment demand for the stock.
Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) fell 5.82% as selling pressure intensified across the semiconductor industry. With Nvidia scheduled to report earnings tomorrow, investors are becoming increasingly cautious about elevated chipmaker valuations and the sustainability of AI infrastructure spending.
This week's corporate earnings could prove pivotal in determining whether the recent sell-off represents a temporary correction or the beginning of a more sustained downturn. Nvidia's earnings on November 17 will provide critical insight into the strength of AI infrastructure demand, particularly as investors reassess elevated semiconductor valuations, escalating capital expenditures, and restrictions on chip exports to China. With Bitcoin also falling to its lowest level since July, weakness across speculative assets suggests investors are becoming increasingly selective about where they allocate capital.
Beyond technology, Walmart's November 19 earnings report will offer an important assessment of consumer spending habits heading into the holiday shopping season. Persistent inflation and elevated borrowing costs could increasingly strain household budgets, threatening corporate revenue growth and profitability. With the 10-year Treasury yield now above 5%, businesses face a more challenging financing environment while investors have increasingly attractive alternatives to equities. For a sustainable year-end recovery to materialize, markets will likely need evidence that AI investment remains productive, consumer spending remains resilient, and inflationary pressures are beginning to ease.

items.summary: There's Now a 100% Chance of a Fed Rate Hike in December -- but That's Not the Worst News for Wall Street  The Motley Fool</
items.content:
Though the Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite have hit several new highs this year, elevated inflation has become a serious problem.
Following a better-than-expected October jobs report, the CME Group’s proprietary FedWatch Tool now pegs the chance of a December rate hike at 100%.
The pace of the Federal Open Market Committee’s (FOMC) rate-hiking cycle may be about to pick up.
Last month, the stock market celebrated the fourth anniversary of the artificial intelligence (AI)-driven bull market. The AI infrastructure build-out has helped propel the Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI -1.41% ) , S&P 500 ( ^GSPC -1.92% ) , and Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC -2.49% ) to several record highs in 2026.
But expecting this parabolic rally to continue may be wishful thinking .
While the Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite have lengthy track records of rallying over multiple decades, their short-term performance can be dicey. Thanks to persistently elevated inflation, caused in part by Trumpflation (inflation derived from President Donald Trump's policies), Wall Street's bull market may be running on borrowed time.
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and the FOMC may be weeks away from a more aggressive rate-hiking cycle. Image source: Official Federal Reserve Photo.
According to a new prediction, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh and the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) are likely to raise interest rates next month -- but this isn't the most damaging news for the stock market.
The FOMC is expected to hike interest rates on Dec. 9
Although no predictive tool can guarantee what the FOMC will do on Dec. 9, the CME Group 's ( CME +0.44% ) FedWatch Tool has a remarkably accurate track record of forecasting future changes in the federal funds target rate .
Based on 30-day Fed Funds futures prices as of Nov. 12, the CME Group's proprietary tool puts the odds of a rate hike at 100% in a little over three weeks. For added context, the odds of a rate hike stood at 67% one week prior, on Nov. 5.

This increase in rate-hike probability follows a stronger-than-expected October jobs report that saw 165,000 nonfarm payroll jobs added, and the unemployment rate ease slightly to 4.1%. While a strong economy is generally a good thing for corporate America, it suggests that persistently elevated inflation won't ease anytime soon without action from the Federal Reserve.
In addition to a hot jobs report, President Trump’s tariff and trade policy, coupled with the ongoing Iran war, have become entrenched in the U.S. economy. It's a lot tougher for the central bank to combat entrenched inflationary pressures .
Fed Governor Christopher Waller has opened the door to a 50-basis-point rate hike. Image source: Official Federal Reserve Photo.
The prospect of an ongoing Fed rate-hiking cycle is worrisome for a historically expensive stock market whose No. 1 catalyst, the AI infrastructure build-out, is being financed by debt. If borrowing costs continue to climb, even a marginal slowdown in the AI data center build-out could lead to growth-rate and valuation-premium re-ratings that send the Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite over the edge.
But what's even more important to Wall Street is the pace of this rate-hiking cycle.
Fed governor Chris Waller said he's leaning toward supporting a December rate increase even if Tuesday’s inflation report shows improvement—and if it doesn't, then he says a 50 bps move should be on the table.
Last week, while speaking in London, Fed Governor Christopher Waller proclaimed that "more robust action" would be needed if October inflation came in ahead of expectations (and it did). He added:
In that case, I believe a 50-basis-point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting. Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take. In other words, not only are the odds of a December rate hike now at 100%, but the probability of a 50-basis-point hike, rather than 25 basis points, is rising. An aggressive rate-hiking cycle would likely wallop the tech stocks that have led the stock market higher.

items.title: Ashes of exiled Nobel Laureate Miguel Ángel Asturias returned to Guatemala
items.summary: The poet, writer and diplomat died in Europe in 1974 having been forced to leave his native country.
items.content:
Image caption, The urn was placed in soil brought from different parts of Guatemala in a ceremony honouring the long-exiled poet, author and diplomat
By Vanessa BuschschlÃ¼ter Latin America online editor
The remains of writer and diplomat Miguel Ãngel Asturias have been buried in his native Guatemala 52 years after he died in exile.
His ashes were brought to Guatemala from Paris, where he had lived before his death from cancer in the Spanish capital, Madrid, in 1974.
Asturias was awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1967 for his vivid writings, which drew on the experiences of indigenous Guatemalans.
The urn containing his ashes was placed in soil gathered from different parts of Guatemala at a cultural centre named after him in Guatemala City.
His son, whose name is also Miguel Ãngel Asturias, said at the ceremony on Sunday: "I can tell you, old man, that you are with us, you are in your homeland, you will sleep beneath your own skies."
Asturias, who was born in 1899, first moved to Paris in the 1920s to study ethnology.
Influenced by the surrealists, he wrote his first major work, Legends of Guatemala, a retelling of Maya origin legends and mythological tales, while in France.
Subsequent works, such as the 1946 novel The President and his Banana Trilogy, denounced the terrors of dictatorship in Latin America and the exploitation indigenous workers suffered on banana plantations.
Arguably his most famous novel was Men of Maize, published in 1949, which explores the struggles of indigenous communities as the world around them quickly changes and modernises.
Image caption, Nobel Peace Prize laureate Rigoberta MenchÃº (centre) attended a ceremony to welcome the ashes of Asturias back to Guatemala alongside the writer's son (right)
Between 1944 and 1954, a period known as "Guatemala's 10 Years of Spring", he served in several diplomatic posts in Central and South America and continued writing.
But when the democratically elected Guatemalan President Jacobo Ãrbenz GuzmÃ¡n was deposed in a CIA-backed coup in 1954, Asturias was stripped of his Guatemalan citizenship, his books were banned and he had to go into exile.
At Sunday's burial ceremony, Asturias's son said that the writer had "always wanted to be in Guatemala" but "political conditions did not allow him to".
The family only agreed to have the ashes moved from PÃ¨re Lachaise cemetery in Paris to Guatemala after the current progressive president of Guatemala, Bernardo ArÃ©valo, was elected in 2023.
ArÃ©valo praised Asturias at the interment ceremony as "our voice in the world".
"He deserved to rest in the land he named and reinvented in his pages," said ArÃ©valo, whose father Juan JosÃ© appointed Asturias to the diplomatic service when the older ArÃ©valo served as president during the 10 Year Spring.

items.title: Faisal Islam: What's in the Brexit reset food deal and are there trade-offs?
items.summary: EU minister Hamish Falconer insists Britain would have some influence on policy as part of a new deal.
items.content:
Image caption, Some British sausages have faced barriers to being exported to the EU
By Faisal Islam ,Â  Economics editor Â  and Â  Lucy Hooker ,Â  Business reporter
In Boston, Lincolnshire, a supplier of ready meals to Marks & Spencer (M&S) manufactures thousands of portions of spaghetti bolognese to be sent to the retailer's shops in the Republic of Ireland.
Every plastic pallet is meticulously individually tagged with a green-grey label âEireâ.
Every truck full of food sent to European Union countries requires hundreds of pages of forms, checks by vets, expense and delays.
It has cost M&S millions of pounds and is part of that reason the British business shut down 11 French stores in 2021.
Many smaller exporters stopped sending their goods to the EU entirely. Some produce, including sausages and certain types of seafood, were entirely stopped.
All this was the predictable consequence of former Prime Minister Boris Johnsonâs 2020 deal prioritising regulatory freedom over freeflowing goods trade.
That will end with a Brexit "reset" that Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to sign with the EU on Friday.
The government claims it could boost the economy to the tune of Â£5bn a year and cut the cost of food for households.
But will the agreement mean a return to frictionless trade for food with the EU or are there trade-offs and quid pro quos the UK will have to make?
EU affairs minister Hamish Falconer, who is a key negotiator with the bloc, acknowledged a âchoiceâ is being made.
In exchange for being able to export produce such as Lincolnshire sausages to the 27 countries, the flipside is the extent to which the UK will be able to influence EU food policies.
The UK will have a "voice in the room", said Falconer, but no vote. Critics have said a reset will make the UK "a rule taker", not a rule maker.
But Falconer said the UK will be involved in a process to shape the rules.
A Brexit reset would not involve any upfront payments, said Falconer, but made it clear there could well be an "exit clause" in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment.
He said this was "reasonable" to consider what would happen if a future Conservative or Reform government wanted to undo the new arrangements. Both parties have said they would if they were in power.
"The EU is worried about that and you can see why," he said.
The BBC understands that the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place following Brexit.
The prime minister has said he believes there is a "win-win" deal to be had with the EU.
Speaking at a Marks & Spencer food court in central London, Falconer said reducing the cost of importing food "will mean less cost for supermarkets, and I hope that less cost then turns into cheaper produce on the shelves".
He said companies have to currently deal with "pages and pages" of form-filling.
Some exports are rejected for having the wrong colour of ink on forms, or an inaccurate Latin name for cooked meats.
The reset could also mean "tearing up" checks that were introduced on goods flowing from Great Britain to Northern Ireland, following Brexit, he said, as well as separate "Not for EU" labelling.
The whole deal to be signed on Friday is calculated to add 0.4% to UK GDP.
Image source, Marcin Nowak/Anadolu via Getty Images
Image caption, Minister for EU relations Hamish Falconer
Tom Bradshaw, president of the National Farmers' Union, welcomed reduced border inspections and paperwork but said that for the NFU it was "a moment of opportunity and risk" with farmers waiting to see what carve-outs and transitional arrangements would be included.
Trade volumes in food exports to the EU had "fallen significantly - by over a third" since 2019, he said.
But the UK should take a "pragmatic" approach to implementing any new rules.
He raised pesticides and precision breeding - or gene edited crops - as areas where he hoped some compromise would be found.
UK firms are, for example, developing tomatoes engineered to contain extra vitamin D.
Historically the EU has had much stricter rules on gene-editing, but this year relaxed regulations.
Falconer said people would have to "wait and see the detail" in this area.
Another contentious area has been crisp flavourings, with concerns raised that stricter EU rules on certain ingredients might limit the sale of some popular snack flavours in the UK.
"I want to take this opportunity to absolutely stamp down on misinformation about smoky bacon crisps," Falconer said.
Post-Brexit the UK had stayed "pretty closely aligned" to European food safety standards, he said.
Two leading snack brands had already adapted their recipes to accommodate EU rules, an example of the kind of alignment that would happen whether or not there was a reset of UK-EU relations.
"The truth is, almost every business in this country that wants to export food or drink will be aligning with EU rules because it's our biggest market.
"Lots of people, like the good people at Walkers and Frazzles have made these changes already, so I would want to reassure people, particularly smoky bacon fans, it's okay," he said.

items.content:
The Danish PM, Mette Frederiksen (centre), Austrian chancellor Christian Stocker (second left), and Rwandan minister Vincent Biruta (right) in Vienna on Monday. Photograph: Leonhard Föger/Reuters
The Danish PM, Mette Frederiksen (centre), Austrian chancellor Christian Stocker (second left), and Rwandan minister Vincent Biruta (right) in Vienna on Monday. Photograph: Leonhard Föger/Reuters
Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda
Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’
Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.
The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.
In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.
Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.
In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.
Hope Hostel in Kigali was prepared to house asylum seekers sent from Britain to Rwanda under the Conservatives’ prepared scheme. Photograph: AP Unlike the failed scheme pursued by the British Conservative government in Rwanda, or Italy’s agreement with Albania , it will not apply to people pursuing asylum claims.
The reception centre, which would be an open facility, was not intended to house people long term but to accommodate regular flows of people, the countries said. Diplomatic sources said the EU countries were not using British-funded facilities built in Kigali.
The governments involved argue it will protect the European asylum system while removing the incentive for irregular migrants to come to Europe .
Denmark’s immigration minister, Morten Bødskov, whose government has pioneered a tough line on migration widely emulated across the EU, said it was “a huge breakthrough”.
The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said: “Return hubs offer a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe, whose countries of origin do not cooperate in the repatriation process.”
Andy Burnham told reporters last week that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that with interest, learning from what went on in the past. The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”
The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said the return hubs offered ‘a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe’. Photograph: Radek Miča/AFP/Getty Images Critics have highlighted the ethical difficulties of striking an agreement with Rwanda’s repressive government , which was found in 2024 by the US state department to allow state security forces and civilian officials to commit human rights abuses with impunity, while also raising concerns about freedom of expression and forced labour.
The French Green MEP Mélissa Camara denounced the agreement between the five countries and Rwanda as “an agreement of shame” and “a grave moral failing”. She said: “Under this agreement, people will be deported thousands of kilometres away from the European Union , with no guarantees regarding the compliance with their rights.”
Alain Berset, the secretary general of the Council of Europe, the continent’s human rights body, said it was not possible “to be so precise a priori” about what any return hubs proposal meant. Speaking to the Guardian before the announcement, he said all members of the Council of Europe were committed to the European convention on human rights “and this must be the lighthouse” for all discussions on return hubs.
“On concrete cases, then we will have to see if this is compliant with the convention,” he said. He stressed that “all countries must be able to define their migration policy”.
Officials involved in setting up the migration centres expect legal challenges, but say the scheme is grounded in human rights law.
Rights organisations say the scheme is bound to fail. “Member states may call them ‘return hubs’ or even ‘welcome centres’, but no euphemism can hide the violence of uprooting people from the life they’ve been building in Europe, and sending them to a country they don’t even know, without family, networks or meaningful prospects,” said Chiara Catelli of Picum, a pan-European organisation that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants.

Andy Burnham to say Brexit ‘has not worked’ and he will sign new deal with EU
PM to meet European leaders at summit this week aiming to secure agreements that ‘could raise GDP by 0.4%’
Andy Burnham will say on Monday that Brexit “has not worked” and that he will sign a new deal with the EU.
It is the latest in a string of comments by the prime minister criticising Brexit, after he told the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday that the UK has “lost more than we gained” through leaving the EU.
Burnham is due to meet European leaders at a summit this week and secure agreements that he says could raise GDP by 0.4% – about £17bn – including on food and farming, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme.
Speaking at the lord mayor’s banquet in the City of London, Burnham is expected to argue that Boris Johnson’s promise to take back control was not delivered, and that the country was left with a needlessly hard Brexit that created barriers for businesses and damaged its economic potential.
Andy Burnham says UK has ‘lost more than we gained’ through Brexit
“It’s like the Emperor’s New Clothes – where no one is prepared to say the obvious truth. Well, I say it as I see it. And to be frank, the emperor has nothing on,” Burnham will say. “The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained.”
Burnham is to say he will sign an agreement with the EU, so long as it:
Is consistent with the Labour manifesto and the government’s red lines.
It improves the Brexit deal and brings it closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016.
And it passes the so-called “ Makerfield test” by delivering real, tangible improvements in people’s everyday lives.
“This is a win-win,” Burnham is expected to say. “It illustrates our new approach. Not adversarial. No longer burning bridges – but being constructive and positive, showing that we can come together to confront shared challenges.”
However, the EU relations minister, Hamish Falconer, told the BBC on Sunday that the UK could have a “voice in the room” under a new deal with the bloc, but no vote on EU food policies.
He added there could well be an “exit clause” in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment, explaining that the EU was “worried” about the possibility of a future Reform or Conservative government undoing the agreement.
The exit clause, previously nicknamed the “Farage clause” , is designed to guard against any the cost of potentially reversing any reset on Friday should the UK’s political landscape change.
The cost of infrastructure at the borders has largely been paid for by private companies, including Eurotunnel, but French staff the food checks there, at Calais port and at Boulogne-sur-Mer, where all fish checks take place.
Meanwhile, Johnson, the former Conservative prime minister who resigned over Partygate in 2022, has said Britain would “absolutely” vote for Brexit again if Burnham forced another vote on the issue.
He told the Telegraph: “It is madness to escalate the Brexit issue as your political priority. He will impale himself and his party on this point, and he needs to move off it because he won’t win – because the reality is that people are not fools.”
