items.content:
Andy Burnham, Britain’s prime minister, and Ursula von der Leyen, European Commission president, at a summit last week. Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/Pool PA/AP
Andy Burnham, Britain’s prime minister, and Ursula von der Leyen, European Commission president, at a summit last week. Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/Pool PA/AP
Monday briefing: The many stages of the UK-EU relationship – and what’s next
In today’s newsletter: From situationship to a possible makeup, a look at the evolving relationship, and the bloc’s big feelings about the future
Good morning. Ahead of the hotly anticipated UK-EU summit this Friday, Andy Burnham is expected to make the reset of our relationship with Europe the pivotal theme of his white-tie speech at the lord mayor’s banquet in London tonight.
The prospect of closer ties – and the possibility of going “all the way” to reversing Brexit – has been met with jubilation and relief in some quarters and vehement opposition in others, while around Westminster and across the media the psychodrama has been spiralling for weeks.
At this point, I’m reminded of that Robert Burns couplet: “ O wad some Pow’r the giftie gie us / To see oursels as ithers see us! ” What does the EU think about all this? Are they ready to reverse what leading figures have repeatedly described as a colossal act of self-harm? Or are they viewing this latest iteration with bombastic side-eye? I posed these questions to Jennifer Rankin , the Guardian’s Brussels correspondent. First the headlines.
UK news | A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 has waived her right to anonymity to campaign for a staggered age of consent , which would make it illegal for adults over a certain age to have sex with 16- and 17-year-olds.
Youth unemployment | Andy Burnham has pledged to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment before a watershed review, promising “a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world”.
Environment | The strongest El Niño in centuries has added urgency to UN climate talks in Turkey as vulnerable countries face “compounding” crises. In other Cop31 news, queer and gay protesters defied a crackdown on LGBTQ+ rights in Turkey to lead a civil society climate march.
UK news | Two people aged 22 and 23 have died after their car was hit by a BMW being pursued by police . West Yorkshire police said four people had been arrested and appealed for witnesses to come forward.
Air transport | The Trump administration says Friday’s four-hour nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that delayed or cancelled thousands of flight stemmed from routine maintenance . The US transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, blamed prior presidents and Congress for the stoppage.
In depth: ‘This is a real priority for the EU, in almost emotional terms’
While official discussions about the UK rejoining the EU are not on the agenda this week, there is genuine enthusiasm about the matter. Photograph: Andy Rain/EPA Ahead of the summit, the pro-Brexit polity has been in broadcast mode: headlines from the past few days include: “Burnham’s plot to rejoin the EU would leave the average UK household £6,500 poorer” (Express); “Taxpayers funding pro-EU university courses” (Sunday Telegraph); “Staggering cost of PM’s EU reset” (Daily Mail).
Stay Out, a new campaign against rejoining the European Union, launched last week. While the guy you really want to hear from right now – David Cameron, the prime minister who lost the 2016 Brexit referendum – has insisted the UK’s problems have nothing to do with its exit from the EU.
Even within the Labour fold, there are rumblings of unease from MPs and unions.
But the one-day summit in Brussels this Friday does not include any formal discussion of rejoining: instead, the EU and UK hope to sign deals on food and drink, emissions trading and the youth experience scheme (a work and study exchange programme).
Still, the mood music is upbeat. Back in September, when Burnham first opened the door to a Brexit reversal, French president Emmanual Macron responded: “welcome back.” while Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez said: “Spain would welcome Britain’s return with open arms.”
The enthusiasm is genuine, says Jennifer. Indeed, some European diplomats have told her the technicalities could be wrapped up within a year because the UK remains closely aligned with the bloc in so many areas. “It would be such a vote of confidence in the European project for a country to decide to return after voting to leave”.
Situationship: what’s at stake at this week’s summit?
Though Burnham has predicted “some long nights” of negotiation this week, Jennifer says there’s optimism on each side as the first two deals on food and drink and emissions trading were largely agreed.
There are two sticking points with the youth exchange deal. First, the Home Office wants to limit numbers to the UK to keep migration figures low. Second, there’s disagreement over whether those students would pay UK domestic rates of tuition fees or the international rate, which is four or five times higher for some courses.
The UK is offering concessions on tuition fees if it can join Made in Europe, the EU legislation designed to protect domestic manufacturing from cheap Chinese competition. But the EU says it can’t make a deal on Made in Europe this week, because the law is still at a draft stage.
And here’s where it gets complicated. The European Commission has proposed delaying an agreement on tuition fees for six months, which could allow time to get the UK into Made in Europe, a diplomatic win for Britain. But there’s pushback from member states who want to pin down the UK on tuition fees this week. “This is a real priority for the EU, in almost emotional terms,” Jennifer says. “Lots of EU officials and diplomats studied in the UK, or their children did, and they felt this was one of the big losses of Brexit, that these person-to-person links were being eroded.”
On-again, off-again: what else could get in the way of closer working?
In play at Friday’s summit will also be a future deal on Britain’s return to the EU’s internal electricity market and a joint migration pact, with the UK pushing for access to EU crime databases to tackle the small boats crisis.
Member states are already working hard to smooth things out on the electricity front, to stop it becoming a sticking point. A couple of weeks ago, Jennifer reported on leaders from Germany, Denmark and elsewhere calling for deeper cooperation on clean energy – which she reads as an attempt to head off a row about how much the UK should contribute to EU cohesion funds for the evident privilege of cutting red tape, easing trade and, ultimately, reducing costs.
A similar row over UK contributions scuppered negotiations last year on our entry into a €150bn EU defence fund.
It could also be a challenge for the UK to realign with the EU on farming, after changing to a payment model that puts more emphasis on delivering environmental benefits. And past UK governments have been lukewarm about EU AI regulation, devised post Brexit.
Conscious partnership : will the EU welcome future closeness this week?
I learned long ago there’s no such thing as a stupid question, so I ask mine now: will there be a moment on Friday when Ursula von der Leyen offers the equivalent of Macron’s “welcome back” ? Will there be a “just give us six months to sort out the paperwork Andy” vibe?
The European Commission president is, by nature, a cautious politician, Jennifer tells me, so she doesn’t expect anything so specific. “I’m sure she – and António Costa, the European Council president – will get asked about it at the press conference, and they’ll want to send a signal about the UK being welcome to rejoin.”
But behind closed doors, in Brussels and other capitals, what Jennifer hears repeatedly is that it’s up to the UK to decide what it wants. And, while the prospect of Brexiteer Nigel Farage in Downing Street has faded in recent months, there remains a deal of caution about the vicissitudes of UK politics. “Now the Burnham government is exploring the options, but there’s also an awareness that you could have a very different government in a few years’ time,” she says.
It’s not you, it’s me : what else is Europe worrying about?
The EU and its member states are preoccupied with far weightier problems: the war in Ukraine (Volodymyr Zelenskyy attends every EU summit), the rise in support for the far right , street protests , hybrid threats from Russia, a trade deficit with China that has reached a staggering €1bn a day in 2026 .
“There are so many other issues crowding on the agenda,” says Jennifer. So it’s not all about us? “That’s actually been the theme of my decade of reporting from Brussels,” she says with a laugh.
There’s profound concern about the prospect of Marine Le Pen winning the French presidential elections next year, which could tip the bloc into a crisis if she pursues her resolutely anti-EU agenda, which includes reducing France’s substantial contribution to the EU budget.
Beyond that, there’s a broader question about increasingly divided and unstable politics across member states. “Every single member state has to agree to the UK’s re-entry,” Jennifer reminds me. “Who knows what the EU will look like in 2030 when Britain could be having a rejoin referendum?”
Tuesday | The former health and social care secretary Alan Milburn’s long-awaited review into why increasing numbers of young people are falling out of work and education, is expected to be released.
Thursday | German chancellor Friedrich Merz, French president Emmanuel Macron and UK prime minister Andy Burnham will be among around 20 heads of state meeting in Berlin to discuss defence funding for Ukraine, and to establish a unified position on future peace negotiations in its war with Russia.

The i Paper leads with “Pressure grows for new consent law to protect teenagers from adult predators”, Metro has “Rethink on the age of consent”, the Sun writes “Brand’s rant from prison”.
The Telegraph says “Johnson: Britain would back Brexit again”, the Express writes “Brexit U-turn means ‘more asylum seekers’”. The Times has “Zero-hours ban to cost billions”, the Mail has “£80,000 a day spent ferrying migrants around”, the Mirror ’s splash is “Dying in the dark”, and the FT ’s is “Nvidia scandal spurs drive to choke China’s AI chip supply”.
This week, after a 13-year wait, gamers will finally get hold of Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest instalment of the most successful console computer game in history. How did a game of stealing cars and shooting strangers become such an enormous cultural phenomenon? The Guardian’s video games editor, Keza MacDonald , traces the history of games by Rockstar, GTA’s creator, and what its most successful product has told us about the US , the setting of all its games so far.
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad
Hidde Burgmans with an accidental find in Palermo, Sicily. He has used his skills as a digital designer to create a global app for sightings of special trees. Photograph: Nadia Roeleveld Some travellers seek out ancient landmarks when they visit a new place. Hidde Burgmans, from the Netherlands, looks for ancient trees – and he’s created an app of the same name to help people find remarkable old trees around the world, from Malaysian baobabs to the Fortingall yew in Perthshire, Scotland, thought to be an astounding 5,000 years old.
Users can review remarkable old trees around the world, and upload their favourites to the Ancient Trees app . “On Tuesday somebody photographed a tree in Edinburgh. Today, someone in Freiburg,” said Burgmans. “That just makes me happy. I thought it was quite a niche, geeky thing, but apparently more people are interested in ancient trees than I thought.”

Trump Heads To Summit As China Hands Warn His Big Gamble Is 'Backfiring'
President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping in Beijing on May 15, 2026
As President Donald Trump embarks on another major trip to China, a pair of White House Asia policy veterans warned in a piece for The New York Times that his "gamble" on a softer approach to the nation is "backfiring" badly and urged the incoming Democratic Congress to push back.
Mira Rapp-Hooper and Ely Ratner each served in high-ranking Asia policy roles within the Biden administration, and writing for The Times on Monday morning, they explained that, in his second term, Trump seemed to hope that treating China in a more "accommodating" way might encourage them to respond in kind. In reality, however, things have certainly not played out that way.
"The Trump administration has scaled back key military operations in the region and withheld support for Taiwan and U.S. allies facing Chinese coercion," the pair wrote. "The hope has been that such measures would help avert a potential clash with China. But nearly two years into his second term, Mr. Trump’s approach is backfiring, emboldening China to throw its weight around Asia and raising the risk of a military crisis."
They added later: "China’s leaders have long made clear that they want the United States to keep its warships away from China’s coast, end arms sales to Taiwan, leave Beijing’s expansive maritime claims unchallenged, pull American forces from the region and refrain from siding with allies who cross China. Over the past two years, the Trump administration has granted much of that."
In doing so, the pair argued, the Trump administration had hoped it would "buy time for America to reduce its dependence on Chinese rare earths, rebuild the U.S. defense industrial base and manage the war with Iran." Instead, China has refused to let up, continuing to exert pressure on the region and expand its presence.
To address this ballooning issue, Rapp-Hooper and Ratner urged the forthcoming Democratic Congress to act, even if their Republican counterparts remain unwilling to break with the president.
"The Senate also can make confirmation of pending and future appointments to the Pentagon and State Department contingent on a commitment to restoring regular U.S. Navy transits of key waterways in the region and supporting allies facing Chinese intimidation," they explained. "In next year’s annual defense bill, Congress should commit more money to the Pacific Deterrence Initiative , a program it established in 2021 to strengthen America’s military position in the region but which came with no dedicated funding."
They concluded: "A bipartisan approach is more likely to succeed and endure. Leading Democratic and Republican members of Congress have already called on Mr. Trump to release the stalled Taiwan arms package. The midterms offer a chance to go further in restoring America’s commitment to its allies in Asia and rebuilding an approach to the region that actually keeps the peace."

Prediction: A Stock Market Crash Is Coming Eventually. Here's What Investors Should Do Based on What Happened in the Last 3 Crashes.
Over the last few years, both the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) and Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) have benefited enormously from enthusiasm surrounding artificial intelligence (AI). History suggests a downturn is inevitable at some point, though.
While this doesn't mean a crash is coming tomorrow, one useful valuation metric suggests investors should prepare for the possibility of outsize volatility. Let's analyze the last three stock market crashes and see what important lessons we can uncover about what investors should do when stocks eventually plunge.
Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »
The CAPE ratio suggests the stock market is overvalued
Developed by economist Robert Shiller, the cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings (CAPE) ratio compares the S&P 500's current price with its average inflation-adjusted earnings over the last 10 years. By smoothing out fluctuations in earnings per share (EPS), the CAPE ratio provides a longer-term perspective on stock market valuations.
Historically, the CAPE ratio has averaged approximately 18. But as of this writing (Nov. 13), it stands near 41. As the chart below illustrates, this places the stock market among its most expensive periods in history.
For perspective, the CAPE ratio reached 44 in December 1999, right before the dot-com bubble burst. Generally, prolonged readings between 30 and 40 have indicated elevated valuations and, consequently, increased vulnerability to economic shocks.
There is an important caveat to point out. The CAPE ratio does not predict when a stock market crash will occur. Stocks can remain expensive for a long time and valuations can normalize through earnings growth rather than falling share prices.
In addition, not every market crash starts with a rising CAPE ratio. The metric is more useful for evaluating long-term return expectations rather than accurately forecasting short-term market movements.
Nevertheless, today's elevated reading suggests investors should be mindful of the risks associated with paying historically high prices for stocks.
What happened during the last three stock market crashes?
The last three major crashes reveal how painful market downturns can become.
The dot-com crash (2000–2002): Following the collapse of speculative internet companies, the S&P 500 declined 49% between March 24, 2000, and Oct. 9, 2002. The technology-heavy Nasdaq plunged nearly 78% from its peak on March 10, 2000.
The Great Recession (2007–2009): The collapse in the housing market triggered another bear market during the mid-2000s. Between Oct. 9, 2007, and March 9, 2009, the S&P 500 lost 57% of its value while the Nasdaq dropped more than 50%.
The COVID-19 crash (2020): Pandemic-related shutdowns triggered one of the fastest market collapses in history. Between Feb. 19 and March 23, 2020, the S&P 500 cratered 34%. The Nasdaq declined roughly 30% during the same period.
The S&P 500 eclipsed its dot-com peak in May 2007, regained its pre-financial-crisis high in March 2013, and recovered its pre-pandemic record by August 2020. Despite their different causes, all three downturns eventually gave way to recoveries.
What $10,000 invested during these crashes would be worth today
Let's consider what would have happened if an investor bought an S&P 500 index fund near the bottom of each downturn and held that investment through today.
These examples assume an investor purchased shares at the bottom, which is something that's nearly impossible to accomplish consistently. That's not the real takeaway, though.
The lesson here is that investors who held a diversified portfolio and remained invested through periods of uncertainty and volatility were ultimately rewarded by the stock market's resilience.
This is why buy-and-hold investing and a long-term outlook are the most effective strategies for navigating volatility. Investors can also use dollar-cost averaging to purchase stock regularly, reducing the temptation to time market bottoms.
Another stock market crash will eventually occur, although nobody knows when. History shows that investors who avoid emotional panic-selling and maintain a long-term time horizon will be better positioned to benefit from the inevitable recovery.

The Nasdaq Has Entered a Correction. Here Are 3 Space and EV Stocks I’d Buy if It Turns Into a Crash.
The Nasdaq Composite fell 5.5% on Nov. 5 and closed at 24,315, more than 11% below the record it set on Oct. 6. That put the tech-heavy index in a correction per CNBC . The trigger was the Democratic sweep in the Nov. 3 midterms, which stirred fears that new limits on data centers could slow the artificial intelligence (AI) build-out.
Here's a simple way to think about the words getting thrown around. A correction is a 10% drop from a recent high, and it happens often enough that it's closer to bad weather than an emergency. A bear market is a 20% drop. A stock market crash is a rapid, steep decline, typically more than 20% in a matter of days or weeks.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
The Nasdaq has since bounced, closing at 25,466.19 on Nov. 11. I'd rather make my shopping list before the next leg down. These three space and electric vehicle (EV) stocks are already about 40% or more below their highs, and each could come out of a crash stronger.
1. Rocket Lab: Customers are booking a rocket that hasn't flown yet
Rocket Lab (NASDAQ:RKLB) builds small rockets, satellites, and satellite parts. Its Nov. 9 report showed a record quarter: Revenue rose 73% to $268 million, and its backlog, meaning signed work it hasn't delivered yet, jumped 52% in three months to about $3.6 billion.
Then there's Neutron, its bigger reusable rocket. Its first launch slipped to no earlier than 2027, yet satellite operators signed more than $515 million in Neutron contracts last quarter, and Rocket Lab raised the base price to $70 million on several of them.
It's also buying Iridium Communications (NASDAQ:IRDM), the satellite phone and data network, for about $8 billion including debt, adding a steady subscription business. Rocket Lab ended September with $4.4 billion in cash and says the deal is already fully funded. Shares closed at $66.15 on Nov. 11, about 56% below their 52-week high.
BYD Company ADR (OTC:BYDDY) is China's biggest maker of electric vehicles (EVs), and it makes its own batteries. With a brutal price war at home, it's selling abroad. In October, it exported 170,194 vehicles out of the 490,168 it sold.
That push is showing up in profits. Third-quarter revenue rose 13.6% to 221.5 billion yuan ($32 billion), and net profit climbed 28% to about 10 billion yuan ($1.5 billion). It's also bringing Flash Charging to Europe. It can refill BYD's second-generation Blade Battery from 10% to 70% in five minutes, about as long as a stop at the gas pump.
That's why I'd want it in a crash. A profitable carmaker that builds its own batteries can cut prices in a downturn and still make money while weaker rivals run dry. At $8.72, the shares are about 40% below their 52-week high and trade around 17 times earnings.
3. Rivian: The R2 is working, and Volkswagen is helping pay the bills
Rivian Automotive (NASDAQ:RIVN) finally has a cheaper SUV that people want. The R2 became its best-selling vehicle in Q3, helping deliveries jump 46% to 19,248 and revenue rise 38% to $2.16 billion.
The hidden strength is software. Volkswagen pays Rivian, through a joint venture, to build software for VW's future cars. That helped Rivian's software and services business earn a $256 million gross profit last quarter, more than covering its $80 million loss on building vehicles. Next up is "Point to Point," which drives a whole route while the owner supervises, plus an Autonomy and AI Day on Dec. 9.
The catch: Rivian's free cash flow was negative $1.1 billion last quarter, meaning it spent that much more than it brought in. It has about $7.1 billion available, including a $1 billion Volkswagen loan from October. Shares closed at $13.54 on Nov. 11, about 40% below their 52-week high.
Rocket Lab has the cash, BYD has the profits, and Rivian has a partner paying part of its way. In a crash, that's what separates the companies that buy cheap from the ones forced to sell cheap.

Megaspeed, the company linked to the downfall of Nvidia boss, says it’s a ‘legitimate and lawful business’
Company insists Alice Huang, who is accused of being a Chinese spy, left business in late 2025
Elon Musk joins 165,000 others calling for Nvidia to bring back Jensen Huang
Megaspeed International, the company linked to the downfall of the Nvidia chief, Jensen Huang , says it is a “legitimate and lawful business” and has announced that its director, who allegedly had an affair with Jensen Huang, left the business in late 2025.
The Singapore-based cloud computing company on the weekend said it was “aware of recent media reports containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence”.
Megaspeed said it had “retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation”.
A baffling trail from Australia to Singapore: what is Megaspeed, the company implicated in downfall of Nvidia’s Jensen Huang?
Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the chip manufacturer Nvidia after reports of extramarital affairs with Alice Huang and two company employees.
US intelligence agencies believe the tech chief, whose products have been crucial to the AI boom, had been targeted by Alice Huang, the former director of Megaspeed International.
US officials have alleged Alice Huang may have been acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times has reported .
In the past three years, Megaspeed has been one of Nvidia’s biggest foreign customers, buying nearly US$5bn (A$7.4bn, £3.8bn) in AI chips and advanced hardware.
A US senator asked the commerce department to investigate whether Megaspeed had diverted Nvidia chips to China.
Megaspeed said on Sunday it would not comment on Alice Huang’s “personal and private matters”.
“Alice Huang officially left Megaspeed effective August 30, 2025 and currently has no role with the company,” it said in a statement.
Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The global facades of Megaspeed International form a puzzling corporate picture , and involve a lottery retailer in rural Australia, a dilapidated storefront in Kuala Lumpur and a near-empty office in Singapore.
The company on Sunday said: “Megaspeed designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate.”
Short seller Culper Research in May quoted a Megaspeed employee as saying Alice Huang was “still our boss”, in a report accusing Nvidia of having a “China problem”.
Elon Musk joins 158,000 others calling for Nvidia to bring back Jensen Huang in open letter
On Thursday, Singaporean authorities said Alice Huang had been barred from re-entering the city state after a 2025 investigation into the company’s “suspected breaches of our domestic laws”.
The ministry of home affairs said it had held Alice Huang’s passport from June 2025 until February. Police believed she had given them “inaccurate” information, to downplay her role at the company, but released her due to insufficient evidence.
She was issued a stern warning and barred from re-entering the country. Taiwan has also barred her from re-entry, its authorities have said.
Singapore’s initial investigation related to Megaspeed’s potential “false declarations” over the purchase of computer servers.
On Friday, Malaysia said it was investigating a subsidiary of Megaspeed International over the possible diversion of advanced AI chips to other countries.
Megaspeed has previously said there was no evidence of illegal chip transfers.
Its registered Sydney office is home to numerous business and had no Megaspeed signage, mailbox or physical presence when the Guardian visited last week . No one had heard of Megaspeed Australia or its listed director, 29-year-old Kai Kang.
Reuters visited a news agency and lottery retailer, in Seymour, Victoria, an hour’s drive north of Melbourne, where a woman, who identified herself as Kang’s mother, said Kang was based in Shanghai and did not know anything about the Singaporean company.
Kang has not been accused of any wrongdoing. Attempts to contact him were unsuccessful.
The US attorney general, Todd Blanche, said last week that the Justice Department had not concluded whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy.
Asked whether she was a spy, the US president, Donald Trump, said: “I don’t know if that’s been determined yet.”
Beijing rejected the allegations as unsubstantiated. Associated Press was unable to reach Alice Huang for comment. The Guardian has sought comment from Alice Huang.
Megaspeed began as the overseas arm of a Chinese video game developer and was incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International. It adopted its current name in March 2023, when all its shares were transferred to Huang Le Limited, a British Virgin Islands company. Alice Huang is also known by her Chinese name, Huang Le.
By November 2023, she was no longer listed as a Megaspeed director, and all her shares had been transferred to an entity owned by Singaporean businessman Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan.
The company’s finances have also attracted attention. Singapore corporate records show its total assets rose roughly 90-fold from end-2023 to 2024, reaching almost US$3bn (A$4.4bn, £2.3bn).

Image caption, The Nvidia scandal has sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley as well as the political establishment
By Dearbail Jordan ,Â  Business reporter Â  and Â  Lily Jamali ,Â  North America Technology correspondent ,Â  Reporting from Palo Alto, CA
Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says.
Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.
Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in South East Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.
The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.
Megaspeed said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".
It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".
Alice Huang stepped down from her role as director of Megaspeed near the end of 2023, according to Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS but it said she was still "practically in control" of the company.
Alice Huang - who is of no relation to Nvidia's former boss - had been investigated by Singapore authorities in February 2025 as part of the country's probe into Megaspeed and other companies.
Also on Sunday, US Congressman John Moolenaar said that Jensen Huang had agreed to testify before the House Select Committee on China, which he chairs, as well as the Foreign Affairs and the Intelligence committees.
The committees had threatened to issue subpoenas to Jensen Huang if he did not comply with their requests to testify.
Moolenaar told CBS, BBC's US partner, that none were ultimately issued.
Jensen Huang's testimony is expected to take place behind close doors, with the dates still being finalised.
Moolenaar said: "That's going to be a very important meeting to understand to what degree privileged information was accessed, and to what degree this potential alleged Chinese spy influenced Nvidia's philosophy and may have had an influence on some of our policies with respect to AI and export controls."
Separately, a group of tech leaders including Space X's Elon Musk, have been trying to rally support to have Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia's chief executive.
A representative forJensen Huang declined to comment on a report in the Financial Times suggesting that he was discussing a comeback to the firm he co-founded.
The BBC understands that the likelihood of him being reinstated is very low while the company's internal investigations are ongoing.
The move would also face scrutiny from Washington, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling for Nvidia to hire its next chief executive from outside the company.
For the moment, Nvidia's chief financial officer Colette Kress is leading the firm and will present the company's results on Tuesday, 17 November.
On Friday, Bessent blamed the US Commerce Department, led by fellow cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick, for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips.
Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process".
The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals.
Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.
Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang.
Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
Figure caption, Watch: Who is suspected Chinese spy at centre of Nvidia affair investigation?
Nvidia has been banned from selling its advanced semiconductors to China.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.
Megaspeed said it "designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes". It said this includes "US export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate".
China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

Diamondback Energy, Inc. Announces Core Midland Basin Acquisition
Diamondback Energy , Double Eagle , Mergers & Acquisitions , midland basin
(Oil & Gas 360) – MIDLAND, Texas, Nov. 16, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — Diamondback Energy, Inc. ( NASDAQ: FANG ) (“Diamondback” or “the Company”) today announced that it has entered into a definitive purchase agreement to acquire certain subsidiaries of Double Eagle IV Midco, LLC and Double Eagle V Midco, LLC (together “Double Eagle”) in exchange for approximately 15.56 million shares of Diamondback common stock and $2.15 billion of cash, subject to customary adjustments (the “Double Eagle Acquisition”). The cash portion of this transaction is expected to be funded through a combination of cash on hand, borrowings under the Company’s credit facility and/or proceeds from term loans.
“This acquisition is another important step in Diamondback’s continued growth within the Midland Basin. The undeveloped inventory acquired in this transaction significantly increases the operated working interest and net present value of high return projects that we were already going to drill, while also adding more undeveloped inventory to our portfolio throughout the Midland Basin,” stated Kaes Van’t Hof, Chief Executive Officer and Director of Diamondback.
Mr. Van’t Hof continued, “In 2022, as Diamondback gained subsurface understanding of the emerging Barnett zone in the Midland Basin, we decided to combine that understanding with the differentiated land expertise of the Double Eagle team. Today’s deal is the culmination of that successful partnership, with Diamondback buying out the 40% of the partnership we did not already own, known as ‘netting up’ in the oil business. Our confidence in both the quality of the resource and our execution cost structure ahead of large-scale development made this the right time to complete this transaction. Importantly, Diamondback does not need to add a rig or materially alter our development plan as a result of this transaction, ensuring a seamless integration.”
Mr. Van’t Hof continued, “We are also excited to announce early results from our first full-section Barnett development in Spanish Trail in Midland County. At a recent peak, this project, consisting of four 10,000-foot lateral wells, produced approximately 7.5 MBo/d and 37 MMcf/d, exceeding internal expectations for full-field development and in line with delineation wells in the area. These early results further validate our geologic understanding of the play and provide momentum as we execute full-field Barnett development in 2027 and for years to come.”
Cody Campbell and John Sellers, Co-Chief Executive Officers of Double Eagle, commented, “We are pleased to once again partner with Diamondback on this transaction. These assets offer high-quality inventory and meaningful Barnett runway, and we are confident they will be in great hands with an operator that shares our commitment to West Texas. We are proud of what the Double Eagle team has built in the Midland Basin and plan to continue our operating momentum with our multi-rig development program on our remaining assets in Reagan County.”
Approximately 176,000 net acres in the core of the Midland Basin
Estimated 2027 oil production of approximately 35 MBo/d (92 MBoe/d, 38% oil)
68% of the asset is undeveloped with over 1,200 estimated gross (495 net) horizontal locations in primary development targets with an average lateral length of more than 11,500 feet; inclusive of 101 gross (46 net) drilled uncompleted wells
Immediately accretive to all relevant financial metrics including Cash Flow 1 per share, Free Cash Flow 2 per share and NAV per share
1 Cash Flow defined as operating cash flow before working capital changes
2 Free Cash Flow defined as cash flow from operating activities before changes in working capital in excess of cash capital expenditures
Diamondback expects the transaction to close on December 21, 2026, subject to the satisfaction of customary closing conditions.
Jefferies LLC is serving as lead financial advisor to Diamondback, with Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC also serving as financial advisor to Diamondback. Latham & Watkins LLP is serving as legal advisor to Diamondback.
Vinson & Elkins LLP is serving as legal advisor to Double Eagle.
Diamondback is an independent oil and natural gas company headquartered in Midland, Texas focused on the acquisition, development, exploration and exploitation of unconventional, onshore oil and natural gas reserves in the Permian Basin in West Texas. For more information, please visit www.diamondbackenergy.com .

Nvidia ( NVDA -4.12% ) extended its recent sell-off on Monday, November 16, closing at $156.14. New U.S. restrictions on access to advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips added to mounting concerns surrounding the company's leadership transition and long-term growth prospects. Several Wall Street analysts also lowered their price targets ahead of Tuesday's highly anticipated earnings report.
Trading volume surged to 326.6 million shares, approximately 119% above its three-month daily average of 148.9 million, reflecting heightened investor uncertainty. With regulatory and leadership risks mounting, Nvidia's upcoming earnings report will be particularly important in determining whether the company's growth outlook can restore investor confidence.

Wall Street suffered broad losses on Monday as investors reduced their exposure to technology and other growth stocks. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC -1.92% ) fell 1.92% to 7,416, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC -2.49% ) declined 2.49% to 24,510.
Selling pressure was particularly pronounced across the semiconductor industry amid the new restrictions. Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD -5.58% ) plunged 5.58% to $504.28, while Broadcom ( AVGO -3.92% ) dropped 3.92% to $333.40. The widespread losses suggest investors are reassessing the broader AI investment landscape, rather than reacting solely to Nvidia's company-specific challenges. Rising Treasury yields and tighter U.S. export restrictions are adding to concerns about semiconductor valuations and future revenue growth.
Nvidia's earnings report on Tuesday comes at a critical juncture for the chipmaker. Wall Street analysts have been lowering their price targets, reflecting growing concerns about leadership stability, regulatory restrictions, and the sustainability of AI infrastructure spending. The latest U.S. restrictions on remote access to advanced AI chips could further limit Nvidia's addressable market, potentially weighing on future revenue growth.
For Nvidia, strong quarterly results alone may not be enough to reverse the recent sell-off. Investors will be looking for evidence that the company can sustain its revenue growth and profit margins, maintain its technological leadership, and navigate an increasingly restrictive regulatory environment. Management's forward guidance will likely carry more weight than its backward-looking financial results in determining whether the stock can establish a sustainable recovery.

Apple is adding face unlock to the iPhone Duo — without new hardware
Apple is testing a new iPhone Duo feature that would use the front-facing camera to look at your face for authentication.﻿
Apple is testing a new iPhone Duo feature that would use the front-facing camera to look at your face for authentication.﻿
Jay Peters is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.
Apple is working on a face unlock feature for the iPhone Duo that uses the front-facing camera for authentication, and it’s already testing it with the new iOS 27.3 beta released today, as reported by MacRumors . Currently, the only way to unlock the iPhone Duo is by using Touch ID or entering a passcode, which might feel like a step back if you prefer face authentication using the Face ID feature available on other iPhones.
The iPhone Duo’s face unlock feature seemingly has a few caveats, however: it’s only available for the lock screen, you can only use your face for an unlock if you have used Touch ID or input a passcode within 45 minutes, and you can’t use the face authentication for Apple Pay purchases.
iOS 27.3 is set to launch publicly in December, Apple said last month , so should the feature make it to the full release, you may not have to wait too long for it to be officially available.
Apple reportedly wants to add Face ID to the second-generation iPhone Duo, Bloomberg reports .
